chunks.section: What overstriding means
chunks.source: Heiderscheit BC et al. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43(2):296-302
chunks.text: Overstriding means the foot lands far in front of the body, with the knee nearly straight. This acts like a brake at every step and sends more load into the knee and hip. In the app's form check this shows up as "Contact placement": the foot should land closer to under the hips, with the knee slightly bent. Taking slightly shorter, quicker steps is the simplest way to bring the landing point back under the body.

chunks.section: Raising step rate by 5-10% reduces load on knees and hips
chunks.source: Heiderscheit BC et al. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43(2):296-302
chunks.text: In a lab study of 45 recreational runners, raising step rate (steps per minute) by 5% at the same speed reduced the energy the knee had to absorb, and raising it by 10% reduced the load at both the knee and the hip. With more steps, the body bounced up and down less, braking was smaller and the foot landed closer to the body. A small increase of 5-10% from your own natural cadence is enough; big jumps are not needed.

chunks.section: Higher step rate and runner's knee pain
chunks.source: Lenhart RL, Thelen DG, Wille CM, Chumanov ES, Heiderscheit BC. Increasing running step rate reduces patellofemoral joint forces. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2014;46(3):557-564
chunks.text: Pain around or behind the kneecap (patellofemoral pain, "runner's knee") is one of the most common running injuries. This study showed that raising step rate by 10% lowered the peak force on the kneecap joint during running. That is why raising cadence slightly is one of the first form changes physios use for runner's knee, together with strengthening the hips and thighs and adjusting training load.

chunks.section: How to raise your cadence
chunks.source: Willy RW et al. In-field gait retraining and mobile monitoring to address running biomechanics associated with tibial stress fracture. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2016;26(2):197-205
chunks.text: In this study, runners raised their step rate by about 7.5% using simple feedback during their normal outdoor runs, and the lower impact loading was still there a month later. To do it yourself: count your steps for 30 seconds on an easy run and double it to get steps per minute. Set a metronome app 5-7% higher and run with it for a few minutes at a time, several times in a run. Keep the same speed and simply take quicker, shorter steps. After a few weeks the new rhythm feels natural.

chunks.section: There is no perfect cadence of 180
chunks.source: Heiderscheit BC et al. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011;43(2):296-302
chunks.text: The famous "180 steps per minute" comes from watching elite runners at race pace; it is not a target for everyone. Natural cadence changes with speed, height and leg length, and it rises as you run faster. Research supports small changes from your own baseline (about 5-10%) rather than forcing a fixed number. If you have no pain and no clear overstride, you do not need to change your cadence.

chunks.section: Daily carbohydrate depends on how hard you train
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text:
Carbohydrate (rice, chapati, idli, poha, fruit) is the main fuel for running. The joint position stand of the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM), the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Dietitians of Canada sets daily carbohydrate by training load, in grams per kg of body weight:
- Light training or skill work: 3-5 g per kg per day.
- Moderate training, about 1 hour a day: 5-7 g per kg per day.
- Endurance training of 1-3 hours a day at moderate to high intensity: 6-10 g per kg per day.
- Very high load, more than 4-5 hours a day: 8-12 g per kg per day.
Carbohydrate should go up and down with the day's training, so a rest day needs less than a long-run day.

chunks.section: Fat and total energy for athletes
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: Athletes should get about 20-35% of their energy from fat. Going below 20% is not advised, because fat carries vitamins A, D, E and K and essential fatty acids. Energy needs change with body size, training load and the day's sessions. The first goal of an athlete's diet is to eat enough energy to cover training and normal body functions. Eating too little for long periods harms health and performance (see Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport).

chunks.section: The meal before a run or race
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: Before sessions longer than about an hour, a meal with 1-4 g carbohydrate per kg eaten 1-4 hours before helps top up the body's energy stores. Bigger meals need more time to settle. Choose foods that are low in fat, fibre and protein to avoid stomach problems: for example idli with a little chutney, plain dosa, poha, upma, bread with jam or banana, or curd rice. Always use foods you have practised with in training, not new foods on race day.

chunks.section: Carbohydrate loading before a long race
chunks.source: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SHS, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci 2011;29(Suppl 1):S17-S27
chunks.text: For races longer than about 90 minutes (half marathon and marathon), eating 10-12 g carbohydrate per kg per day for the 36-48 hours before the race fills the muscle energy stores (glycogen). Training is cut down (tapered) at the same time. In practice this means bigger portions of rice, chapati, idli, dosa, potatoes, fruit and sweet drinks, and less fibre and fat so the meals are easy to digest. For races shorter than 90 minutes, normal high-carbohydrate eating the day before is enough.

chunks.section: Refuelling fast between two sessions
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: When there are less than 8 hours between two hard sessions, eat about 1.0-1.2 g carbohydrate per kg per hour for the first 4 hours after the first session, in small frequent snacks. Adding protein helps muscle repair. When there is a full day before the next session, normal meals across the day refill energy stores and there is no rush.

chunks.section: Most distance runners land on the heel
chunks.source: Larson P et al. Foot strike patterns of recreational and sub-elite runners in a long-distance road race. J Sports Sci 2011;29(15):1665-1673
chunks.text: When runners were filmed in a marathon, about 89% landed heel-first at the 10 km point and about 93% by the 32 km point, as they got tired. Even many fast runners land on the heel. Heel striking is therefore the normal pattern for distance runners and is not, by itself, a mistake.
chunks.docTitle: Foot strike: heel, midfoot or forefoot

chunks.section: No foot strike is best for everyone
chunks.source: Hamill J, Gruber AH. Is changing footstrike pattern beneficial to runners? J Sport Health Sci 2017;6(2):146-153
chunks.text: This review found no strong evidence that changing from a heel strike to a midfoot or forefoot strike prevents injuries or makes running more economical for most runners. Changing foot strike moves the load rather than removing it: a forefoot strike puts less load on the knee but more on the ankle, calf and Achilles tendon. Where the foot lands relative to the body (overstriding) matters more than which part of the foot touches first.
chunks.docTitle: Foot strike: heel, midfoot or forefoot

chunks.section: Heel striking and injury in one college team
chunks.source: Daoud AI et al. Foot strike and injury rates in endurance runners: a retrospective study. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2012;44(7):1325-1334
chunks.text: In a Harvard college cross-country team, runners who mostly landed on the heel reported about twice the rate of repetitive stress injuries compared with those who mostly landed on the forefoot. This was a small, backward-looking study in one team, so it shows a link, not proof that heel striking causes injury. It is one reason some coaches suggest a softer, flatter landing for runners with repeated knee or shin problems.
chunks.docTitle: Foot strike: heel, midfoot or forefoot

chunks.section: How to change foot strike safely
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text: Experts in this review use foot-strike change for some specific injuries, not for every runner. If you change towards a midfoot landing, do it slowly: start with short sections (for example 1 minute in every 5) on easy runs, add calf raises to strengthen the calf and Achilles, and expect some calf soreness at first. Stop and get advice if you get Achilles or foot pain. Often simply taking shorter, quicker steps makes the landing flatter by itself.
chunks.docTitle: Foot strike: heel, midfoot or forefoot

chunks.section: How much carbohydrate to take per hour during a run
chunks.source: Jeukendrup A. A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise. Sports Med 2014;44(Suppl 1):S25-S33
chunks.text:
How much carbohydrate you need during exercise depends mainly on how long it lasts:
- Under about 45 minutes: no carbohydrate is needed; water is enough.
- About 45-75 minutes: small amounts, or even just rinsing the mouth with a sports drink, can help.
- 1-2 hours: up to about 30 g per hour.
- 2-3 hours: up to about 60 g per hour.
- More than about 2.5 hours: up to about 90 g per hour, but only using a mix of glucose and fructose and only if the gut has been trained to take it.
Start fuelling early in the run, in small regular amounts (for example every 15-20 minutes), rather than waiting until you feel tired.
chunks.docTitle: Fuel during long runs and races

chunks.section: Indian foods and drinks for fuel during long runs
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: The ACSM position stand says carbohydrate during exercise can come from drinks, gels, chews or normal foods, as long as the athlete tolerates them. Cheap Indian options with about 25-30 g carbohydrate each: 1 ripe banana; 3-4 dates; 500 ml of homemade drink with 2 tablespoons of sugar or glucose powder and a pinch of salt; 2 tablespoons of raisins; a small boiled sweet potato. On hot days or runs longer than 90 minutes, a drink with some salt (or ORS) is better than plain water.
chunks.docTitle: Fuel during long runs and races

chunks.section: Training the gut and avoiding stomach problems
chunks.source: Jeukendrup AE. Training the gut for athletes. Sports Med 2017;47(Suppl 1):101-110
chunks.text: Stomach cramps, bloating, nausea and running to the toilet are common in distance runners. The gut can be trained: practising your race-day food and drink during long training runs improves how well carbohydrate is absorbed and reduces stomach problems. Meals high in fibre, fat or protein just before running raise the risk, as does dehydration. Never try a new gel, drink or food for the first time on race day.
chunks.docTitle: Fuel during long runs and races

chunks.section: Race morning breakfast
chunks.source: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SHS, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci 2011;29(Suppl 1):S17-S27
chunks.text: A carbohydrate-rich meal 1-4 hours before a race tops up the liver's energy store after the overnight fast. For early-morning races (5-6 am starts) most runners eat a small, familiar, low-fibre snack 1-2 hours before: 2-3 idlis, a banana with 2 slices of bread and jam, or a bowl of poha, with a glass of water. Go lighter if you are nervous or the start is very early. A practised carbohydrate drink is an option for runners who cannot eat solid food early.
chunks.docTitle: Fuel during long runs and races

chunks.section: Getting used to running in the heat (acclimatisation)
chunks.source: Racinais S et al. Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. Br J Sports Med 2015;49:1164-1173
chunks.text: The body adapts to heat with repeated training in hot conditions: sweating starts earlier, heart rate is lower and the body stays cooler. Most of the change happens in the first week and it is largely complete in about two weeks, with daily sessions of about 60-90 minutes in the heat. During that time, reduce pace and distance and build up slowly. The adaptation fades over a few weeks without heat exposure. Even when adapted, performance in the heat is lower than in cool weather, so adjust pace targets.
chunks.docTitle: Running in Indian heat, and muscle cramps

chunks.section: Planning runs on hot days
chunks.source: Racinais S et al. Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. Br J Sports Med 2015;49:1164-1173
chunks.text: On hot and humid days, run early in the morning or late in the evening, wear light clothing, use shaded routes and carry water or plan water stops. Humidity matters as much as temperature, because sweat cannot evaporate well in humid air. Cold drinks and ice slurries before and during exercise, and pouring cool water on the head and neck, help keep body temperature down. Slow down when the heat index is high, and cancel hard sessions in extreme heat.
chunks.docTitle: Running in Indian heat, and muscle cramps

chunks.section: Warning signs of heat illness and first aid
chunks.source: Casa DJ et al. National Athletic Trainers' Association position statement: exertional heat illnesses. J Athl Train 2015;50(9):986-1000
chunks.text: Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency. Warning signs are confusion, strange behaviour, stumbling, collapse, and a very high body temperature (above 40 degrees C). Other signs of heat illness include headache, dizziness, nausea, chills and goosebumps in the heat. Stop running at once. For suspected heat stroke the rule is "cool first, transport second": cool the whole body as fast as possible, ideally in cold water or with ice water and wet towels, while calling for medical help. Heat stroke treated with fast cooling is almost always survivable.
chunks.docTitle: Running in Indian heat, and muscle cramps

chunks.section: Why muscle cramps happen during running
chunks.source: Schwellnus MP et al. Increased running speed and previous cramps rather than dehydration or serum sodium changes predict exercise-associated muscle cramping: a prospective cohort study in 210 Ironman triathletes. Br J Sports Med 2011;45:650-656
chunks.text: Cramps during exercise are often blamed on dehydration or low salt, but research does not strongly support this. In a study of 210 Ironman triathletes, those who cramped were not more dehydrated and did not have lower blood salt. Cramping was linked to racing faster than usual (relative to training) and to a history of cramps. Muscle fatigue is the most likely main cause. Practical steps: pace yourself sensibly, train at race pace so the muscles are ready, and stretch the cramping muscle gently when it happens. Salt and fluid still matter for long hot runs, but they are not a guaranteed cure.
chunks.docTitle: Running in Indian heat, and muscle cramps

chunks.section: Pelvic drop and hip control
chunks.source: Noehren B, Hamill J, Davis I. Prospective evidence for a hip etiology in patellofemoral pain. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2013;45(6):1120-1124
chunks.text: When one hip drops while the other leg is in the air (pelvic drop), the thigh of the standing leg moves inward (hip adduction). In this study, female runners who later developed runner's knee (patellofemoral pain) had more hip adduction during running before they got injured. An earlier study by the same group linked the same pattern with iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome on the outer knee. In the app's form check this appears as "Pelvic level" or "Pelvic stability". Weak hip muscles on the side of the body (gluteus medius) are a common reason.
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: Knee falling inward
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text: When seen from the front, the knee should stay roughly in line with the hip and the second toe while the foot is on the ground. A knee that falls inward (dynamic knee valgus) often goes together with pelvic drop and is a pattern experts target in runners with knee pain. Useful cues: "knees pointing forward", "run with the feet slightly wider apart, as if on two lines", and "squeeze the buttocks a little when you land". In the app's form check this appears as "Knee & foot tracking".
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: Strength alone may not change running form
chunks.source: Willy RW, Davis IS. The effect of a hip-strengthening program on mechanics during running and during a single-leg squat. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2011;41(9):625-632
chunks.text: In this study, six weeks of hip strengthening made the hip muscles stronger and improved single-leg squat control, but did not change how the runners moved during running. A later study by the same group found that gait retraining with a mirror, where runners practised keeping the pelvis level and the knee in line, did reduce hip adduction and knee pain, and the change lasted. So strength work is useful, but to change running form you also need to practise the new movement while running.
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: Hip strength exercises for runners
chunks.source: Willy RW, Davis IS. The effect of a hip-strengthening program on mechanics during running and during a single-leg squat. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2011;41(9):625-632
chunks.text: Simple exercises that target the side and back of the hip, done 2-3 times a week: side-lying leg raises (3 sets of 12-15 each side), clamshells with a band, side plank (3 x 20-40 seconds each side), glute bridges and single-leg bridges (3 x 10-12), single-leg squats to a chair or step-downs from a low step, keeping the knee over the second toe (3 x 8-10 each side). Do them slowly and with good control. Combine them with short running drills where you focus on keeping the hips level.
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: Side-to-side differences (asymmetry) are common
chunks.source: Zifchock RA, Davis I, Higginson J, Royer T. The symmetry angle: a novel, robust method of quantifying asymmetry. Gait Posture 2008;27(4):622-627
chunks.text: Research on gait shows that most healthy runners have some difference between their left and right sides, so perfect symmetry is not normal or necessary. A side-to-side difference matters more when it is large, when it is getting bigger over time, when it follows an injury, or when it comes with pain on one side. In the app, "Stride symmetry" or "Side-to-side rhythm" compares the two sides; use it to track change over time, not as a diagnosis.
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: Improving balance between the two legs
chunks.source: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB. The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med 2014;48:871-877
chunks.text: Single-leg exercises train each side on its own so the weaker side cannot hide: single-leg balance (30-45 seconds, progress to eyes closed or on a pillow), single-leg calf raises, step-ups, split squats and single-leg bridges. Start with the weaker side and match the reps on the stronger side. This meta-analysis found that strength training and balance (proprioception) training both lowered sports injury risk, so this work helps both symmetry and injury prevention.
chunks.docTitle: Pelvic drop, knee tracking and side-to-side symmetry

chunks.section: How much water to drink in a day
chunks.source: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies. Scientific opinion on dietary reference values for water. EFSA Journal 2010;8(3):1459
chunks.text: The European Food Safety Authority sets adequate total water intake at about 2.5 litres a day for men and 2.0 litres a day for women in a mild climate. This includes the water in food, which gives about 20% of the total. Athletes need more: on top of the daily amount, they must replace what they lose in sweat during training. Hot and humid weather, as in much of India, raises sweat losses a lot.

chunks.section: Drinking before training
chunks.source: Sawka MN et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand: exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39(2):377-390
chunks.text: Start training well hydrated. About 4 hours before exercise, drink about 5-7 ml per kg of body weight (for a 60 kg runner, about 300-420 ml). If you pass no urine or it is dark, drink another 3-5 ml per kg about 2 hours before. Starting early leaves time to pass extra urine before the session. A little salt in food or drink before exercise helps the body hold on to the water.

chunks.section: Drinking during training and testing your sweat rate
chunks.source: Sawka MN et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand: exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39(2):377-390
chunks.text: Sweat rates vary from about 0.5 to more than 2 litres per hour between people and with the weather. The aim during exercise is to avoid losing more than 2% of body weight from water loss, because that starts to hurt endurance performance. You can measure your own sweat rate: weigh yourself before and after a 1-hour run (without clothes, after passing urine), add the water you drank, and the loss in kg is roughly your sweat loss in litres per hour. Do not drink so much that you gain weight during exercise.

chunks.section: Salt and sports drinks for long or hot runs
chunks.source: Sawka MN et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand: exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39(2):377-390
chunks.text: Sweat contains salt (sodium), on average about 35 mmol per litre with a wide range between people. For long sessions, heavy sweaters and hot weather, the ACSM suggests drinks with about 20-30 mmol per litre of sodium and 5-10% carbohydrate. A homemade version: 1 litre of water with about 1/4 level teaspoon of salt (about 1.5 g) and 4-5 level tablespoons of sugar or glucose. Lemon or a little juice can be added for taste. Store-bought ORS also works for long hot runs. Salty food after the session (dal, sambar, curd rice with salt) helps replace losses.

chunks.section: Drinking after training
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: To fully replace water lost in sweat, drink about 1.25-1.5 litres for every 1 kg of body weight lost during the session, spread over the next few hours rather than all at once. The extra 25-50% covers urine losses. Eating salty food or drinking a salty drink with it helps the body keep the water. When there is plenty of time before the next session, normal meals and drinks usually restore hydration.

chunks.section: Danger of drinking too much water (hyponatraemia)
chunks.source: Hew-Butler T et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Clin J Sport Med 2015;25(4):303-320
chunks.text: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia means the blood salt (sodium) level falls too low. The main cause is drinking more water or sports drink than you sweat out, especially in slower runners in long events. Signs include headache, swelling of hands, nausea, vomiting, confusion and, in severe cases, fits. It can be fatal. The consensus advice is to drink according to thirst, and never to drink "as much as possible". Gaining weight during a race is a warning sign of overdrinking.

chunks.section: Checking hydration with urine colour
chunks.source: Armstrong LE et al. Urinary indices of hydration status. Int J Sport Nutr 1994;4(3):265-279
chunks.text: Urine colour is a simple daily check of hydration. Pale straw or light lemon coloured urine suggests good hydration; dark yellow or brown urine, or passing very little urine, suggests you need to drink more. Some vitamins (B vitamins) can turn urine bright yellow, and first-morning urine is darker, so use the check through the day. Feeling very thirsty is another sign to drink.

chunks.section: Protein in common Indian foods
chunks.source: Longvah T et al. Indian Food Composition Tables 2017. ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad
chunks.text:
Approximate protein in usual Indian servings, based on the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT 2017):
- 1 katori cooked dal, chana or rajma (from about 30 g dry): about 7 g.
- 1 glass (250 ml) milk: about 8 g. 1 katori curd: about 5 g.
- 50 g paneer: about 9 g. 100 g tofu: about 8-10 g.
- 25 g dry soya chunks (1 small katori cooked): about 13 g.
- 1 egg: about 6 g. 100 g cooked chicken: about 25 g. 100 g fish: about 20 g.
- 30 g peanuts or roasted chana: about 6-7 g. 1 katori sprouts: about 5 g.
- 1 chapati: about 3 g. 1 cup cooked rice: about 4 g. 2 idlis: about 4 g.
Cereals give some protein too, but on their own they are not enough for an athlete.

chunks.section: Carbohydrate in common Indian foods
chunks.source: Longvah T et al. Indian Food Composition Tables 2017. ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad
chunks.text:
Approximate carbohydrate in usual Indian servings (IFCT 2017 values with common portion sizes):
- 1 cup (about 150 g) cooked rice: about 45 g.
- 1 medium chapati: about 15 g. 1 plain dosa: about 20 g. 1 idli: about 8 g.
- 1 plate poha or upma: about 40 g.
- 1 banana: about 25-27 g. 3 dates: about 18 g. 1 medium sweet potato: about 25 g.
- 2 slices of bread: about 26 g. 1 tablespoon sugar or jaggery: about 12 g.
Whole grains and millets (brown rice, ragi, jowar, bajra) give more fibre and minerals; on the day before a race or just before a run, lower-fibre choices like white rice, idli and banana sit better in the stomach.

chunks.section: A balanced Indian plate for an athlete
chunks.source: ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition. Dietary Guidelines for Indians. Hyderabad, 2024
chunks.text: The ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) recommend a varied plate: plenty of vegetables, green leafy vegetables and fruits; whole cereals and millets; pulses, beans, eggs, fish or meat; milk or curd; and a small amount of nuts, seeds and oil. They advise limiting ultra-processed foods high in fat, sugar and salt. For an athlete, the same plate works with bigger cereal portions on heavy training days and a protein food (dal, curd, paneer, egg, soya, chicken or fish) at every meal.

chunks.section: Combining cereals and pulses for better protein
chunks.source: Rogerson D. Vegan diets: practical advice for athletes and exercisers. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:36
chunks.text: Cereals (rice, wheat, millets) are low in the amino acid lysine, and pulses (dal, chana, rajma) are low in methionine. Eating them together across the day gives a more complete protein. Traditional Indian combinations already do this: dal rice, rajma chawal, idli or dosa with sambar, khichdi, chapati with chana, and pesarattu. Adding curd or milk to a vegetarian meal improves protein quality further.

chunks.section: Cheap protein for hostel, budget and travel
chunks.source: Longvah T et al. Indian Food Composition Tables 2017. ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad
chunks.text: Some of the cheapest protein sources per gram in India are soya chunks, eggs, peanuts, roasted chana, sprouts, dals, milk and curd. In a hostel mess, take an extra katori of dal, curd or the egg option, and keep roasted chana, peanuts or a packet of milk as snacks. While travelling, good options are curd rice, idli sambar, boiled eggs, roasted chana, peanut chikki, bananas and milk or buttermilk.

chunks.section: Limit salt in normal meals, add it for long sweaty runs
chunks.source: World Health Organization. Guideline: sodium intake for adults and children. Geneva: WHO, 2012
chunks.text: The WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 g of salt (about 1 level teaspoon, or 2 g sodium) per day to protect the heart and blood pressure. Many Indian diets go above this through pickles, papad, namkeen and packaged snacks. Athletes who sweat a lot lose salt in sweat and may need some extra salt around long or hot training sessions, but the everyday diet should still avoid very salty processed foods.

chunks.section: Trunk position: a slight forward lean
chunks.source: Teng HL, Powers CM. Influence of trunk posture on lower extremity energetics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015;47(3):625-630
chunks.text: How much the upper body leans forward changes where the load goes. In this study, running with a little more forward trunk lean reduced the load on the knee (the kneecap joint) and moved more of the work to the hip muscles. Running very upright or leaning back puts more load on the knee. A good cue is to "run tall and lean slightly forward from the ankles, not from the waist", keeping the chest open. Bending forward at the waist is not the same thing and can strain the lower back.

chunks.section: Why arm swing matters
chunks.source: Arellano CJ, Kram R. The metabolic cost of human running: is swinging the arms worth it? J Exp Biol 2014;217:2456-2461
chunks.text: Arm swing balances the twisting of the legs and saves energy. When runners in this study ran without swinging their arms, they used about 3% more energy with arms held behind the back, about 9% more with arms across the chest and about 13% more with hands on the head. So a free, relaxed arm swing is part of efficient running. Swing the arms forward and back from the shoulder with elbows bent at about 90 degrees, hands loose, and avoid crossing far over the middle of the body.

chunks.section: Head, neck and gaze
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text: There is little direct research on head position, so this is based on common coaching and expert practice. The head should stay level and steady, eyes looking ahead about 10-20 metres, neck relaxed, jaw loose. Dropping the head to look at the feet or pushing the chin forward adds tension in the neck and shoulders and can pull the trunk out of position. Big side-to-side head movements usually come from the arms crossing the body or from tiredness, so fixing arm swing often fixes the head.

chunks.section: Running economy: less bounce, less braking
chunks.source: Folland JP, Allen SJ, Black MI, Handsaker JC, Forrester SE. Running technique is an important component of running economy and performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017;49(7):1412-1423
chunks.text: In a study of 97 runners, technique was clearly linked with how much energy runners used (running economy) and with their race performance. Bouncing up and down a lot (high vertical movement of the pelvis) and braking strongly at each landing were among the features linked with poorer economy. Practical cues: run "low and smooth", let the foot land closer under the body, and keep a quick, light rhythm rather than big bounding strides.

chunks.section: How much protein an athlete needs in a day
chunks.source: Jager R et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:20
chunks.text: For most people who exercise, 1.4-2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is enough to build and keep muscle. The ACSM joint position stand gives a similar range of 1.2-2.0 g per kg. Endurance runners usually need the middle of the range. People doing heavy strength training, or trying to keep muscle while eating less, need the top end. Getting enough protein across the whole day matters more than any single meal or the exact timing.

chunks.section: Athletes need more protein than the general Indian RDA
chunks.source: ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition. Nutrient Requirements for Indians: Recommended Dietary Allowances and Estimated Average Requirements. Hyderabad, 2020
chunks.text: The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein for healthy Indian adults is about 0.83 g per kg of body weight per day (ICMR-NIN 2020). This is meant for people who do not train hard. Athletes in regular training need clearly more, about 1.4-2.0 g per kg per day. Many Indian vegetarian diets built mainly on rice or wheat fall short of this unless dal, milk, curd, paneer, soya, eggs or meat are added at most meals.

chunks.section: How much protein per meal and how often
chunks.source: Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA. How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2018;15:10
chunks.text: Muscle repair works best when protein is spread across the day, not eaten in one big meal. The ISSN advises about 0.25 g per kg (roughly 20-40 g) per meal, every 3-4 hours. For people who want to build muscle, Schoenfeld and Aragon suggest about 0.4 g per kg per meal across at least four meals, which adds up to about 1.6 g per kg per day. In practice: include a protein food in breakfast, lunch, the evening snack and dinner.

chunks.section: Protein after training
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: About 0.3 g protein per kg of body weight soon after a key session (within about 0 to 2 hours), and again every 3-5 hours, supports muscle repair. After a run, pair the protein with carbohydrate, for example curd rice, milk with banana, egg with chapati, or dal rice. The idea of a strict 30-minute "window" is overstated: if a meal with protein was eaten 1-2 hours before training, the next meal can come a little later without harm.

chunks.section: Protein before sleep
chunks.source: Jager R et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:20
chunks.text: Eating about 30-40 g of slowly digested protein (casein, which is the main protein in milk) 30 minutes or so before sleep can increase overnight muscle repair. For an Indian athlete, a glass of milk with dinner or before bed, curd, or paneer at dinner does a similar job using normal food.

chunks.section: Protein for vegetarian and vegan athletes
chunks.source: Rogerson D. Vegan diets: practical advice for athletes and exercisers. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:36
chunks.text: Plant proteins usually have less of some essential amino acids (lysine in cereals, methionine in pulses) and are digested a little less well. Vegetarian and vegan athletes can still meet their needs by eating a mix of protein foods through the day (cereal plus pulse, as in dal rice, rajma chawal, idli sambar, chapati with chana) and by aiming for the higher end of the protein range. Good Indian plant sources are soya chunks, tofu, chana, rajma, moong and other dals, peanuts and seeds. Vegans should also plan for vitamin B12, iron, calcium, zinc and iodine.

chunks.section: Protein powders: ICMR advice and contamination risk
chunks.source: Maughan RJ et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med 2018;52:439-455
chunks.text: The ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2024) advise against using protein supplements to build body mass, and recommend getting protein from food. The IOC consensus statement on supplements says protein powders can be convenient but are not needed when food intake is enough. It also warns that supplements, including protein powders, are sometimes contaminated with banned substances. For a competitive athlete this can cause a failed dope test, because the athlete is responsible for anything found in their body. Food first: milk, curd, paneer, eggs, dal, soya, chicken or fish.

chunks.section: Principles of gait retraining
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text: Experts in this review agree that form changes should be simple and practised a little at a time. Change one thing at a time with one simple cue ("quicker steps", "run quietly", "knees forward"). Use feedback (a metronome, a mirror on a treadmill, or video) at first, then slowly take it away so the new pattern becomes automatic. Start with a few minutes inside easy runs and build up over 2-6 weeks. Expect some new muscle soreness, but stop if you get sharp pain.

chunks.section: Drills for quicker steps and a better landing
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text:
Common coaching drills to practise landing under the body with a quick rhythm (based on coaching practice, before easy runs or after a warm-up):
- Metronome runs: 4-6 x 2 minutes on an easy run at 5-7% above your normal step rate.
- Strides: 4-6 x 80-100 m, relaxed and fast, walking back to recover, focusing on quick light steps.
- A-march and A-skip: 2-3 x 20 m, knee up, foot landing under the hip.
- Quick feet (fast small steps on the spot or over 10 m): 3 x 10 seconds.
- "Run quietly" cue: on an easy run, try to make your foot strikes as quiet as possible for 1-minute periods; quieter landings usually mean softer loading.

chunks.section: Drills for posture, arms and hips
chunks.source: Barton CJ et al. Running retraining to treat lower limb injuries: a mixed-methods study of current evidence synthesised with expert opinion. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:513-526
chunks.text:
Coaching drills to practise good posture and control (based on coaching practice):
- Wall lean drill: lean against a wall with a straight body from ankles to head, then march, to feel the forward lean coming from the ankles. 3 x 20 seconds.
- Arm swing drill: sit or stand and swing the arms from the shoulders, elbows at 90 degrees, hands brushing the hips, not crossing the middle. 3 x 30 seconds.
- Single-leg balance with a level pelvis in front of a mirror: 3 x 30-45 seconds each side.
- Mirror running on a treadmill: watch that the pelvis stays level and the knees point forward, a few minutes at a time.
- Wide-step running cue: run as if each foot lands on its own line, for 1-minute periods, if the knees fall inward.

chunks.section: Calf and foot strength for runners
chunks.source: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR. Effects of strength training on the physiological determinants of middle- and long-distance running performance: a systematic review. Sports Med 2018;48(5):1117-1149
chunks.text: The calf muscles and Achilles tendon take very high loads with every running step. Strong calves help running economy and protect the shins and Achilles. Simple exercises 2-3 times a week: double-leg calf raises building to single-leg calf raises (3 sets of 15-20 each side, slowly), bent-knee calf raises for the deeper calf muscle, skipping or pogo hops (3 x 20 seconds) once strength is good, and toe yoga or towel scrunches for the foot muscles.

chunks.section: How much sleep athletes need
chunks.source: Hirshkowitz M et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary. Sleep Health 2015;1(1):40-43
chunks.text: The US National Sleep Foundation recommends 7-9 hours of sleep a night for adults aged 18-64 and 8-10 hours for teenagers aged 14-17. Athletes in hard training often benefit from the upper end, and a short afternoon nap can help on heavy days. Keep a regular sleep and wake time, keep the room dark and cool, and avoid screens, heavy meals and caffeine late in the evening.
chunks.docTitle: Sleep, recovery and the menstrual cycle

chunks.section: More sleep can improve performance
chunks.source: Mah CD, Mah KE, Kezirian EJ, Dement WC. The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep 2011;34(7):943-950
chunks.text: In a Stanford study, college basketball players tried to sleep about 10 hours a night for 5-7 weeks. Their sprint times got faster, shooting accuracy improved by about 9%, and they reported better mood and less tiredness. The study was small, but it suggests many athletes are not sleeping as much as their bodies need, and that more sleep is a simple, free way to recover better.
chunks.docTitle: Sleep, recovery and the menstrual cycle

chunks.section: Short sleep and injury risk
chunks.source: Milewski MD et al. Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes. J Pediatr Orthop 2014;34(2):129-133
chunks.text: In a study of young athletes, those who usually slept less than 8 hours a night were about 1.7 times more likely to get injured than those who slept 8 hours or more. Poor sleep also slows reaction time and recovery and raises the chance of getting ill. When training gets harder, protecting sleep is as important as food.
chunks.docTitle: Sleep, recovery and the menstrual cycle

chunks.section: Training and the menstrual cycle
chunks.source: McNulty KL et al. The effects of menstrual cycle phase on exercise performance in eumenorrheic women: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2020;50:1813-1827
chunks.text: A review of 78 studies found that performance may be slightly lower in the early part of the cycle (around the period), but the effect is small and differs a lot between women. There is no need to stop training during periods. A better approach is to track your own cycle and symptoms (cramps, tiredness, mood, sleep) and adjust training on days you feel poor. Periods that stop, become very irregular or very heavy are not normal for athletes and need a doctor's check, as they can signal under-fuelling or low iron.
chunks.docTitle: Sleep, recovery and the menstrual cycle

chunks.section: Food first: which supplements have real evidence
chunks.source: Maughan RJ et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med 2018;52:439-455
chunks.text: The IOC consensus statement says a good diet comes first, and very few supplements improve performance. Those with good evidence in some situations are caffeine, creatine, dietary nitrate (beetroot juice), beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate. Each works only for certain kinds of events and has side effects for some people. Supplements such as iron or vitamin D are useful only when a blood test shows a deficiency. Young athletes in particular should focus on food, training and sleep, and use supplements only with advice from a sports doctor or sports dietitian.

chunks.section: Contaminated supplements and failed dope tests
chunks.source: Maughan RJ et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med 2018;52:439-455
chunks.text: Some supplements, including protein powders, "fat burners" and "muscle gainers", are contaminated with banned substances such as steroids or stimulants that are not listed on the label. Under anti-doping rules (WADA, and NADA in India) athletes are strictly responsible for anything found in their sample, so a contaminated product can cause a ban. Athletes who are tested should avoid supplements unless needed, use batch-tested products, and check with a sports doctor.

chunks.section: Caffeine from coffee and chai before training
chunks.source: Guest NS et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2021;18:1
chunks.text: Caffeine can make endurance exercise feel easier and improve performance. The ISSN position stand says benefits are seen with moderate amounts taken about 60 minutes before exercise, and that lower amounts can also help. People respond very differently: some get a racing heart, anxiety, stomach upset or poor sleep. Everyday sources are filter coffee, instant coffee and chai (chai has less caffeine than coffee). Avoid caffeine late in the day because it harms sleep, try it in training before using it in a race, and children and teenagers should avoid caffeine supplements and energy drinks.

chunks.section: How common running injuries are
chunks.source: Videbaek S, Bueno AM, Nielsen RO, Rasmussen S. Incidence of running-related injuries per 1000 h of running in different types of runners: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med 2015;45(7):1017-1026
chunks.text: This review found that new (novice) runners get about 17.8 injuries per 1000 hours of running, while regular recreational runners get about 7.7 per 1000 hours. Beginners are more than twice as likely to get injured for the same running time, mostly because bones, tendons and muscles have not yet adapted. Beginners should build up slowly, and use walk-run sessions at first.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: How fast to increase weekly running
chunks.source: Nielsen RO et al. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2014;44(10):739-747
chunks.text: In this study of new runners, those who increased their weekly distance by more than about 30% over two weeks had a higher risk of some injuries, such as runner's knee, ITB syndrome, shin pain and hip and hamstring injuries. A separate trial (Buist 2008) found that following the strict "10% rule" did not lower injury compared with a normal programme. The message: avoid big jumps in weekly distance, build gradually, and include easier weeks every 3-4 weeks.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: Strength training prevents injuries; stretching does not
chunks.source: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB. The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Br J Sports Med 2014;48:871-877
chunks.text: This meta-analysis of randomised trials found that strength training reduced sports injuries to less than a third, and balance training reduced them by about half. Stretching had no clear effect on injury risk. Stretching can still feel good and help mobility, but it should not replace strength work. Two short strength sessions a week (squats, lunges, calf raises, bridges, planks) are a good base for runners.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: Strength training makes runners faster
chunks.source: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR. Effects of strength training on the physiological determinants of middle- and long-distance running performance: a systematic review. Sports Med 2018;48(5):1117-1149
chunks.text: This review found that adding strength training (heavy weights and jumping or plyometric exercises) to running improves running economy, meaning the runner uses less energy at the same speed, typically by about 2-8%, and improves time-trial performance. Most studies used 2-3 sessions a week for 6-14 weeks. Strength training did not make runners bulky or slower when done alongside their running.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: Keep most runs easy
chunks.source: Seiler S. What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2010;5(3):276-291
chunks.text: Successful endurance athletes in many sports do about 80% of their training sessions at a low, easy intensity (you can talk in full sentences), and about 20% at hard intensity. Running every session hard leads to tiredness and injury without better results. For most runners this means 1-2 hard sessions a week (intervals, tempo or race), and the rest easy runs, plus a long run at easy pace.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: Bone stress injuries: warning signs
chunks.source: Warden SJ, Davis IS, Fredericson M. Management and prevention of bone stress injuries in long-distance runners. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2014;44(10):749-765
chunks.text: A bone stress injury (including a stress fracture) builds up when bone is loaded faster than it can repair. Warning signs are pain in one spot on a bone (for example the shin, foot or hip) that gets worse with running, tenderness when you press that spot, and later pain while walking or at night. Risk is higher with sudden increases in training, past bone stress injury, under-fuelling, low calcium or vitamin D, and in female runners with missed periods. Stop running and see a doctor; it usually needs rest from running and a scan.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: Achilles tendon pain: load it, do not just rest it
chunks.source: Alfredson H, Pietila T, Jonsson P, Lorentzon R. Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. Am J Sports Med 1998;26(3):360-366
chunks.text: Long-lasting Achilles tendon pain in runners usually improves with slow, heavy calf exercise rather than complete rest. In this classic study, runners did slow heel drops off a step (3 sets of 15 with the knee straight and 3 sets of 15 with the knee bent, twice a day for 12 weeks), and all returned to running. Mild discomfort during the exercise was accepted. This should be done with a physiotherapist's guidance; sudden sharp pain, a snap or swelling needs a doctor.
chunks.docTitle: Training load, strength work and injury prevention

chunks.section: What REDs (under-fuelling) means
chunks.source: Mountjoy M et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med 2023;57:1073-1097
chunks.text: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) happens when an athlete eats too little energy for the training they do, for a long time. The body then has too little energy left for normal functions such as hormones, bones, immunity, and repair. It can happen by accident (not knowing how much training costs, a busy schedule, poor appetite after training) or on purpose (dieting to be lighter). It affects both female and male athletes of all levels.
chunks.docTitle: Under-fuelling and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)

chunks.section: Warning signs of under-fuelling
chunks.source: Mountjoy M et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med 2023;57:1073-1097
chunks.text:
Signs that an athlete may be eating too little for their training include:
- Missed, irregular or stopped periods in women (this is not a normal effect of training).
- Low sex drive or low morning erections in men.
- Bone stress injuries or stress fractures, especially repeated ones.
- Getting ill often, feeling tired all the time, poor sleep, low mood or irritability.
- Performance getting worse despite training, and slow recovery.
Anyone with these signs should see a doctor or sports physician and a sports dietitian.
chunks.docTitle: Under-fuelling and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)

chunks.section: Energy availability and how to avoid under-fuelling
chunks.source: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. ACSM, AND and Dietitians of Canada joint position: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(3):543-568
chunks.text: Energy availability is the energy left for the body after subtracting the energy used in training, expressed per kg of fat-free (lean) mass. About 45 kcal per kg of lean mass per day supports health. Earlier research used about 30 kcal per kg as a warning line, though the 2023 IOC statement says no single cut-off fits everyone. To avoid under-fuelling: eat more on heavy training days, do not skip meals around training, carry snacks on long days, and do not combine heavy training with strict dieting. Weight loss for sport should only be done slowly and with a sports dietitian.
chunks.docTitle: Under-fuelling and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)

chunks.section: Anaemia is common in India and hurts running
chunks.source: International Institute for Population Sciences. National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India fact sheet. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2021
chunks.text: According to the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21), about 57% of Indian women aged 15-49 and about 25% of men are anaemic. Anaemia means too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen, and the most common cause is low iron. For runners it causes tiredness, breathlessness and poor performance. Female athletes, vegetarians and runners who train a lot are at higher risk. A simple blood test (haemoglobin and ferritin) is the way to know; iron tablets should only be taken on a doctor's advice.
chunks.docTitle: Iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12

chunks.section: How to get more iron from Indian food
chunks.source: Sim M et al. Iron considerations for the athlete: a narrative review. Eur J Appl Physiol 2019;119:1463-1478
chunks.text: Iron from meat, fish and eggs is absorbed better than iron from plant foods. Vegetarian sources include green leafy vegetables, rajma, chana, lentils, soya, bajra, jaggery, dates and seeds. Vitamin C (lemon, amla, guava, orange, tomato) eaten in the same meal helps absorption, while tea and coffee taken with or just after a meal reduce it, so keep tea about an hour away from meals. After hard exercise a hormone called hepcidin rises for about 3-6 hours and lowers iron absorption, so iron-rich meals work better in the morning or soon after training than many hours later.
chunks.docTitle: Iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12

chunks.section: Calcium and bone health
chunks.source: ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition. Nutrient Requirements for Indians: Recommended Dietary Allowances and Estimated Average Requirements. Hyderabad, 2020
chunks.text: ICMR-NIN (2020) sets the calcium RDA for Indian adults at 1000 mg per day. Calcium, along with enough energy and vitamin D, is needed for strong bones, which matters for runners because of the repeated impact. Good sources are milk and curd (about 250-300 mg in a glass of milk), paneer, ragi (much higher in calcium than rice or wheat), sesame seeds (til), green leafy vegetables and small fish eaten with bones. Vegans can use ragi, tofu set with calcium, sesame and fortified foods.
chunks.docTitle: Iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12

chunks.section: Vitamin D in athletes
chunks.source: Owens DJ, Allison R, Close GL. Vitamin D and the athlete: current perspectives and new challenges. Sports Med 2018;48(Suppl 1):3-16
chunks.text: Vitamin D helps the body use calcium and supports bones and muscles. Low vitamin D is common in athletes, especially those who train indoors, train very early or late, cover most of their skin, or have darker skin, so it is common even in sunny countries like India. Few foods contain much vitamin D (egg yolk, oily fish, fortified milk). Sensible sun exposure helps. Supplements should be based on a blood test and a doctor's advice, because very high doses can be harmful.
chunks.docTitle: Iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12

chunks.section: Vitamin B12 for vegetarians and vegans
chunks.source: Rogerson D. Vegan diets: practical advice for athletes and exercisers. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017;14:36
chunks.text: Vitamin B12 is found naturally almost only in animal foods. Lacto-vegetarians get some from milk, curd and paneer, while vegans get almost none and need fortified foods or a B12 supplement. Low B12 causes tiredness, anaemia, tingling in hands and feet and poor concentration. A blood test is worth doing if a vegetarian athlete feels tired all the time.
chunks.docTitle: Iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12
